name: BMS-564929
lead: BMS-564929 (also PS-178990) is a potent, orally active, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by Bristol-Myers Squibb for age-related functional decline in men.[1][2] SARMs are designed to give the muscle-building signal of testosterone with less stimulation of the prostate and other tissues, which is why compounds in the class draw interest from people who want more lean mass and a fuller, more muscular physique.[3]

A 2007 Endocrinology study reported a subnanomolar androgen receptor affinity, selectivity over other steroid receptors, and strong stimulation of skeletal muscle with comparatively little prostate stimulation in castrated rats.[1] It advanced to early clinical trials, but Wikipedia reports that the phase I trial was discontinued, and no results were identified.[2][3]

The compound is unapproved, and the World Anti-Doping Agency has prohibited SARMs in sport since January 2008.[2][3] Most published work on BMS-564929 is the rat characterisation and analytical chemistry for doping detection; no human efficacy data exist, so what follows describes the preclinical record and the class context.
infobox: Investigational; trial discontinued; banned in sport since 2008

paras: BMS-564929 is a highly potent androgen receptor agonist with no significant interaction with sex hormone-binding globulin or aromatase, and in castrated rats it was substantially more potent than testosterone at stimulating the levator ani muscle while being much more selective for muscle over prostate.[1] An X-ray crystal structure revealed binding contacts in the ligand-binding domain that differ from those of the native hormones, important for recruiting coregulatory proteins; the authors said further experiments excluded other mechanistic explanations for the tissue selectivity.[1] Wikipedia reports a Ki of 2.1 nM and about 20-fold functional selectivity for muscle over prostate.[2]
The compound suppresses luteinizing hormone strongly, reportedly about 33 times more than testosterone does, which Wikipedia notes could be a concern in human use.[2]

The wider tissue-selectivity rationale for SARMs is that in muscle and bone, where coactivator proteins are abundant, they act as agonists, whereas in tissues dominated by corepressors, such as the prostate, they act as partial agonists or antagonists; SARMs are also not converted by 5-alpha-reductase to the more potent DHT. Wikipedia notes this selectivity is still debated.[3]

Non-steroidal SARMs first appeared in 1998, from a University of Tennessee group and from Ligand Pharmaceuticals, building on the idea, inspired by tamoxifen-type SERMs, of tissue-selective androgens that keep the anabolic benefits of steroids while avoiding androgenic side effects.[3] Bristol-Myers Squibb's team published the characterisation of BMS-564929 in 2007 and framed it as a potential alternative to testosterone, whose drawbacks include prostate stimulation and an inconvenient route of administration.[1] A T Nation forum thread from 2007 quoted the abstract under the title 'No More Injections?', showing that interest from lifters began soon after publication.[7]

No studies found reporting human results for BMS-564929. The 2007 paper states the compound had been advanced to clinical trials for age-related functional decline, and Wikipedia describes it as holding US Investigational New Drug status with a phase I trial reported discontinued.[1][2]

For class context, enobosarm (ostarine), the most studied SARM, has been tested in over 1,700 people across 25 studies at 1 to 18 mg daily according to its manufacturer; a phase III trial increased lean mass without a significant improvement in physical function, and regulators have not accepted lean mass alone as proof of benefit. Adverse events in trials were generally mild and infrequent.[3] Published research on BMS-564929 otherwise consists of the rat study, mass spectrometry of hydantoin-derived SARMs and urine detection methods.[1][4][5][6]

No human safety data were published for this compound. Reviews of the class describe elevated liver enzymes, lowered HDL cholesterol and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (lower gonadotropins, testosterone and SHBG in a dose-dependent manner) in some trials, with enobosarm described as among the least suppressive, and case reports link recreational SARM use to liver injury.[3] Cardiovascular risk is unknown.[3]

SARMs are sold on the gray market as research chemicals; a study cited by Wikipedia found most online products were mislabeled, and some non-SARM compounds are sold as SARMs. The US FDA states that SARMs are unapproved and cannot legally be marketed as supplements or drugs, and criminal convictions in the US and a large fine in Australia have followed marketing them for human consumption.[3] WADA has banned the class since 2008 and has reported positive tests since 2010, with enobosarm and LGD-4033 most commonly detected; screening methods for hydantoin-derived SARMs, including BMS-564929, have been developed.[3][4][5][6]

timeline.event: Pharmacological and structural characterisation of BMS-564929 in rats published; trial discontinued reported by Wikipedia.[1][2]
WADA bans the SARM class; urine detection methods for BMS-564929 described.[3][5]

lore.intro: Discussion of BMS-564929 in lifting communities is sparse; an early 2007 T Nation thread quoted the Endocrinology abstract, and the compound is otherwise discussed within broader SARM conversations.[7]

claims.claim: A potent oral SARM could replace testosterone injections for muscle gain
claims.believers: The 2007 T Nation thread title 'No More Injections?' reflects the hope that an oral, muscle-selective compound could stand in for injected androgens.[7]
claims.experts: The compound's published results are in castrated rats; its phase I trial was reported discontinued, and no human results are available.[1][2]

claims.claim: SARMs build muscle without the side effects of steroids
claims.believers: Wikipedia notes that athletes are drawn to SARMs hoping for anabolic effects with fewer side effects than anabolic steroids.[2]
claims.experts: Class reviews describe elevated liver enzymes, lower HDL and HPG-axis suppression in some trials, and for this compound strong LH suppression has been reported.[2][3]

card.summary: A very potent Bristol-Myers Squibb SARM that stalled in early trials; rat data only.
card.note: Trial discontinued; strong LH suppression reported; banned in sport.

quick.overview:
BMS-564929 is a highly potent experimental SARM built by Bristol-Myers Squibb for age-related muscle and hormone decline.

Rat results were striking, but the early human trial was discontinued and no results are public.
quick.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor very tightly, driving muscle growth in rats while stimulating the prostate less.
quick.risks: Human safety is unpublished. It suppresses luteinizing hormone strongly, is unapproved and is banned in sport.

chain: Binds the androgen receptor with very high affinity
Stimulates skeletal muscle growth in animal models, with less prostate stimulation
Hoped-for lean mass and strength gains
angle.text: BMS-564929 was built to build muscle by activating the androgen receptor in muscle more than in the prostate. Its muscle effects have been shown in rats, and in lifting circles SARMs are discussed as a route to more lean mass; no human results exist for this compound.
